holidays.name: National Card Playing Day
holidays.description: Shuffle up and deal! Dig out the deck and play whatever you like, whether that's poker, rummy, Go Fish or a cutthroat family game of Crazy Eights. It's a good excuse to hold a post-holiday game night with relatives who are still hanging around.
holidays.origin: This is an unofficial observance of unclear origin. It falls in the quiet stretch between Christmas and New Year's, when families are gathered and looking for entertainment.
holidays.funFact: A standard 52-card deck is often said to mirror the calendar: 52 cards for 52 weeks, 4 suits for 4 seasons, and 12 face cards for 12 months.

holidays.name: National Short Film Day
holidays.description: A day for celebrating movies that get to the point. Short films can pack a whole story, a laugh or a gut punch into a few minutes. Pick a few to watch, or make your own on your phone.
holidays.origin: The observance honors the anniversary of the first commercial public film screening. The Lumière brothers held it in Paris on December 28, 1895. Their program was made up of very short films.
holidays.funFact: The Lumière brothers' 1895 screening included a film of workers leaving a factory that lasted under a minute. Some early audiences reportedly flinched at the footage of an oncoming train.

holidays.name: Endangered Species Act Day
holidays.description: A day to celebrate the U.S. law that protects threatened wildlife and the habitats they depend on. Learn about a local at-risk species, support a conservation group, or just spend time outdoors appreciating nature.
holidays.origin: President Richard Nixon signed the Endangered Species Act into law on December 28, 1973. The law has been credited with helping save species such as the bald eagle from extinction.
holidays.funFact: The bald eagle, the national bird of the United States, was once listed as endangered under the Act. It has since recovered enough to be removed from the list.
